title: subscriber: preserve span timing across reloads
body:
## Motivation

A span created while `FmtSpan::CLOSE` is enabled receives timing state that must remain balanced for the span's lifetime. Currently, enter and exit bookkeeping is instead gated by the layer's current configuration.

This breaks in either direction when the configuration changes between an enter and its matching exit:

- If a span is entered before `CLOSE` is disabled, its exit is skipped. Re-enabling `CLOSE` before the span closes leaves it marked busy, causing the debug-build panic reported in [#3529](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/issues/3529) and misclassifying the final interval in release builds.
- If a span is entered while `CLOSE` is disabled and exited after it is re-enabled, the enter is skipped but the exit is recorded, underflowing the nesting count.

Replacing the whole formatter layer has the same problem because timing state stored in an existing span can outlive the layer that created it.

## Solution

Track the number of live timing extensions independently of the current formatter configuration. While any exist, enter and exit callbacks look for timing state on the affected span and update it when present.

Spans created while `CLOSE` is disabled still receive no timing state. The additional bookkeeping only preserves state already attached to an existing span.

The timing implementation has also been moved into a private `fmt::timing` module. This keeps the state machine, accumulated durations, snapshots, display formatting, and focused tests together as one small coherent component. This is similar to the internal refactoring proposed in [#3038](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/pull/3038), without introducing the separate public timing layer proposed in [#2946](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/issues/2946) and explored in [#3063](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/pull/3063).

A few implementation details are intentional:

- `TimingState` preserves the nested-enter behavior introduced in [#2944](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/pull/2944), while representing either `Idle` or a non-zero busy depth.
- `enter` and `exit` accept the clock as `impl FnOnce() -> Instant`, so nested transitions update only the nesting depth and do not sample the clock.
- The live-span count belongs to timing extensions rather than formatter configuration because those extensions can outlive the layer configuration that created them.

Unlike [#3570](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/pull/3570), this keeps lifecycle accounting balanced across configuration changes rather than tolerating missed transitions.

## Tests

The first commit adds characterization tests which intentionally assert the existing panics for both configuration-change orderings. The fix then changes those same tests to assert successful close output. Additional tests cover whole-layer replacement and nested enter/exit accounting.

## Performance

Paired Criterion measurements on this machine:

| Case                                            | Before   | After      |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------: | ---------: |
| Timing unused                                   | 12 ns    | 12 ns      |
| Normal timed span                               | 96 ns    | 94–96 ns   |
| Nested timed enter                              | 42 ns    | 43–44 ns   |
| Existing timed span while `CLOSE` is disabled   | 30–31 ns | 105–106 ns |
| New untimed span while timed spans remain alive | 30–31 ns | 61 ns      |

The existing-span case previously skipped the timing update entirely. Its corrected 105–106 ns cost is close to the 94–96 ns normal timed path, plus the reload layer and conservative extension lookup.

When no timed spans remain alive, the disabled path is unchanged.

Fixes [#3529](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/issues/3529).

title: core: snapshot the dispatcher registry before rebuilding interest
body:
## Motivation

Same bug as #3614: while exactly one `Dispatch` is registered,
`Rebuilder::JustOne` resolves a cold callsite's interest with
`dispatcher::get_default`, the current thread's default, not the
registered dispatch. If the dispatch is not installed yet (#2874) or is
installed on another thread (#3611), `NoSubscriber` answers
`Interest::never()` and the callsite caches it for the life of the
process.

The shortcut exists because `register_dispatch` holds the registry
write lock while it runs subscriber callbacks, so a cold callsite hit
from inside `register_callsite` could not take the read lock. Every
other subtlety in this area follows from that one choice: the
lock-free single-dispatch path, the wrong-thread lookup, the
re-entrancy guard that only exists for scoped defaults, and the race
between a cold-callsite store and a concurrent registration.

## Solution

Remove the choice instead of patching around it.

* **Never hold the registry lock across a callback.** `rebuilder()` and
  `register_dispatch` copy the live dispatches out under the lock and
  release it before `on_register_dispatch` or `register_callsite` run.
  A plain blocking `read()` is now always safe, and `has_just_one`,
  `JustOne`, and the guard-carrying `Rebuilder` variants go away.
* **Store only against an unchanged registry.** A callsite's interest is
  stored only if the registry generation still matches the snapshot it
  was computed from, checked under the read lock so the check and the
  store are atomic against registration. Otherwise it stores
  `Interest::sometimes()`, and `LevelFilter::TRACE` for the max level:
  never wrong, only re-evaluated on each hit. This also replaces the
  serialization that holding the write lock across the rebuild used to
  provide, so two concurrent registrations cannot overwrite each other's
  results with stale ones.
* **Nested registration is conservative.** A registration nested inside
  a registration on the same thread (a subscriber logging from
  `register_callsite`) stores `sometimes` instead of re-entering the
  subscriber. This works the same under a global and a scoped default;
  the old `get_default` path only guarded the scoped case.

Cost: one `Vec` of `Dispatch` clones per rebuild, on a path that
already walks every registered callsite.

Tests, each in its own binary so no other `Dispatch` in the process
interferes with the ordering:

* `scoped_dispatch_cold_callsite`: the original report.
* `register_callsite_contention`: a `Dispatch` registered while another
  thread is mid-registration of a cold callsite; the stale result is
  stored as `sometimes`, not as the stale value.
* `nested_register_callsite`: a callsite first hit from inside
  `register_callsite` is still delivered to the subscriber afterwards.
* `rebuild_interest_cache_from_event`: a rebuild from inside `event`
  cannot set the max level to `OFF`.
* `no_live_dispatch_cold_callsite`: a dead registry still caches `never`.
* `scoped_register_callsite_deadlock`: `register_callsite` holds a mutex
  and logs, then creates a `Dispatch`. This one passes on main; it
  guards against holding a lock across the callback.

## Relationship to #3614

#3614 is the minimal fix: it keeps `JustOne` and adds `try_read`,
`get_current`, and a guard-held store to make the shortcut safe. This
PR is the alternative that deletes the shortcut. Same tests, same
issues fixed; pick whichever shape you would rather maintain.

Fixes: #2874
Fixes: #3611
Refs: #2400

Claude sessions: https://claude.ai/code/session_01L5xF8ccPJuWG2gCE7JSrNr (original), `bfa252a6-75a8-4171-838f-16741ee523c6` (this change; local session)

title: core: read the registered dispatch when rebuilding callsite interest
body:
## Motivation

While exactly one `Dispatch` is registered, `Dispatchers::rebuilder()`
returns `Rebuilder::JustOne`, and `Rebuilder::for_each` resolves it with
`dispatcher::get_default`: the current thread's default dispatcher, not
the registered one. Those are only the same thing when the one dispatch
is installed on the thread that first hits the callsite.

They differ in two ordinary situations: the dispatch exists but is not
installed yet (`Dispatch::new`, then `with_default`; #2874), or it is
installed on a different thread (#3611). Then `get_default` yields
`NoSubscriber`, whose `register_callsite` returns `Interest::never()`,
and the callsite caches that. Nothing rebuilds it afterwards:
`set_default` and `DefaultGuard::drop` do not rebuild the cache, and
registering a second `Dispatch` clears `has_just_one` and takes the
general path, which is also why the bug hides whenever another live
`Dispatch` exists in the process, such as in a test suite.

## Solution

Resolve `JustOne` from the registry, and never store a guess:

* `rebuilder()` upgrades the one registered dispatch under `try_read`
  and drops the guard before any callback runs, so a subscriber that
  creates a `Dispatch` or logs from `register_callsite` cannot deadlock
  on the registry lock or on its own state.
* `for_each` runs the callback through `get_current`, which keeps the
  scoped re-entrancy guard the old `get_default` path had, and reports
  whether the dispatch was actually consulted.
* The store happens inside `with_current`. For `JustOne` that re-reads
  the registry and holds the read guard across `set_interest` and
  `set_max`; the general paths already hold it. If the registry could
  not be read, changed since the snapshot, or the dispatch was not
  consulted, the callsite gets `Interest::sometimes()` and the max
  level `TRACE`: never wrong, only re-evaluated on each hit. If the
  registry has no live dispatch, the callsite gets `never` and the max
  level `OFF`, checked the same way, so a process that is not tracing
  keeps its early-out.

The last point is what makes a concurrent `register_dispatch` safe
(thanks @darkraider01). Its rebuild snapshots the callsite list head
before walking it, so it can miss a callsite pushed during the walk,
and even when it visits one its store can lose to a stale one. Holding
the read guard across the store makes the check and the store atomic
with respect to registration.

Tests, each in its own binary because any other live `Dispatch` in the
process clears `has_just_one` and masks the single-dispatch path:

* `scoped_dispatch_cold_callsite`: the original report.
* `register_callsite_contention`: a callsite first hit while another
  thread holds the write lock gets `sometimes`, then that registration's
  rebuild sets the precise value.
* `nested_register_callsite`: a callsite first hit from inside
  `register_callsite` is still delivered to the subscriber afterwards.
* `rebuild_interest_cache_from_event`: a rebuild from inside `event`
  cannot set the max level to `OFF`.
* `no_live_dispatch_cold_callsite`: a dead registry still caches `never`.
* `scoped_register_callsite_deadlock`: `register_callsite` holds a mutex
  and logs, then creates a `Dispatch`. This one passes on main; it
  guards against holding the read guard across the callback.

Fixes: #2874
Fixes: #3611
Refs: #2400


## Alternative

#3615 deletes the `JustOne` shortcut instead of making it safe: the
registry is snapshotted before any callback runs and stores are checked
against a registry generation. Same tests, same issues fixed; pick
whichever shape you would rather maintain.

title: "Error reading the log directory/files" always fires the first time
body:
## Bug Report

### Version

0.2.5

### Platform

All

### Crates

tracing-appender

### Description

The error `Error reading the log directory/files: No such file or directory (os error 2)` is always printed on first use, when the log directory doesn't exist yet.

This happens when using the [`RollingFileAppender`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L87) with [`max_files`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L112) set, because [`prune_old_logs`](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L655) is [called when `max_files` has a value](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L616), without taking into account if this is the first or nth time that gets executed.

The following snippet should help reproducing the error.

```rust
let file_appender = RollingFileAppender::builder()
        .rotation(Rotation::DAILY)
        .max_log_files(1)
        .filename_suffix("suffix".to_string())
        .build("some_folder");
```

I would expect this error not to appear for the first time, given that the folders won't exist. A possible solution would be to not send any message to `stderr` when the folder doesn't exist. That means the error would never appear when the folder doesn't exist. Doesn't mind if it's the 1st or nth execution.

title: decrease amount of generated code from most macros
body:
This decreases the amount of code generated from most event-generating macros in the crate. Mainly, it does this by deduplicating some calls to `$crate::valueset_all!` and turning the `level_to_log` macro into a function.

## Motivation

When profiling build times for a set of large enterprise crates, I noticed (with `-Zmacro-stats`) that tracing macros took up a large percentage of the generated code. So I went to fix it.

These changes improve compile times by 2-5% across a few different debug configurations in these aforementioned crates.

I would recommend reviewing this with [whitespace disabled](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/pull/3608/changes?w=1) - it becomes a lot easier to understand.

title: journald: normalize events from the log bridge
body:
## Motivation

Events that reach `tracing-journald` through `tracing_log::LogTracer` carry the static `log` callsite. The journal record then reads `TARGET=log` with no `CODE_FILE`/`CODE_LINE`, while the real values ride along as `LOG_TARGET`, `LOG_FILE`, `LOG_LINE`, `LOG_MODULE_PATH` fields (or `F_LOG_*` with the default field prefix). Anything that filters or groups on `TARGET` sees one bucket named `log` for every `log`-crate dependency.

`tracing-subscriber`'s fmt layer already solves this with `NormalizeEvent::normalized_metadata()` and by skipping the `log.*` fields; the journald layer did not.

## Solution

Behind a new `tracing-log` feature (on by default, mirroring `tracing-subscriber`), `on_event` takes the metadata from `normalized_metadata()` when present for `PRIORITY`, `TARGET`, `CODE_FILE`, `CODE_LINE`, and `EventVisitor` skips fields whose name starts with `log.`. Without the feature the behaviour is unchanged.

A record from a `log::info!` in `lsm_tree::version::recovery` now reads `TARGET=lsm_tree::version::recovery`, `CODE_FILE=.../recovery.rs`, `CODE_LINE=40`, and no `LOG_*` fields.

Adds `log_bridge_message` to `tests/journal.rs`, following the existing journald-backed tests.

title: fix(attributes): silence clippy print lints on instrument macro expansion
body:
Closes #3597

The `#[instrument]` attribute macro expands user-written `println!`/`eprintln!` calls inside instrumented functions to `::std::io::_print`/`_eprint`. Clippy's `print_stderr`/`print_stdout` lints only match the literal `println!`/`eprintln!` token, not the macro-expansion call site, producing a false positive.

This PR adds `#[allow(clippy::print_stdout, clippy::print_stderr)]` to the wrapper function emitted by the `#[instrument]` macro. This is the most surgical fix: it covers both sync and async wrappers, and only suppresses the two specific lints that are known to misfire on macro-expanded code.

Verified locally: `cargo check -p tracing-attributes` passes and all 64 tests across the integration test files (`instrument`, `async_fn`, `err`, `levels`, `fields`, `names`, `ret`, `follows_from`, `parents`, `targets`, `destructuring`) pass. `cargo expand` confirms the allow attribute is now present on every generated wrapper fn.

appender: fix latest symlink for relative paths
body:
## Motivation

`latest_symlink` used the full relative log path as its target. Since the link itself lives inside the log directory, a relative directory such as `./logs` produced a target that resolved through the log directory twice.

Fixes #3599

## Solution

Use the log filename as the symlink target so it resolves relative to the directory containing the link. Add a regression test that creates the appender from a relative directory and reads through the resulting symlink.

Tested with:
- `cargo test -p tracing-appender --all-features`
- `cargo check --all --tests --benches`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`

title: RUSTSEC-2026-0258: h2 unbounded empty DATA frames
body:
> h2 unbounded empty DATA frames

| Details             |                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Package             | `h2`                      |
| Version             | `0.3.27`                   |
| URL                 | [https://github.com/hyperium/hyper/security/advisories/GHSA-q83h-524g-xf6h](https://github.com/hyperium/hyper/security/advisories/GHSA-q83h-524g-xf6h) |
| Date                | 2026-08-17                         |
| Patched versions    | `>=0.4.16`                  |

The h2 crate, used internally by hyper, had a flaw that would accept and queue empty DATA frames without limit.
If streams were not actively drained, this could lead to unbounded memory usage, or a panic if the length overflows.

Low severity.

Patched in v0.4.16.

See [advisory page](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0258.html) for additional details.

title: subscriber: add opt-in field value truncation wrapper
body:
## Motivation

Closes #2474. `tracing-subscriber`'s formatters currently write field values in full, which can flood logs when a field (e.g. a large payload, a big `Debug` struct) is unexpectedly long.

## Approach

Per @hawkw's guidance on the issue, this implements truncation as a `MakeVisitor`/`FormatFields` wrapper in `tracing_subscriber::field`, alongside the existing `debug`, `display`, and `delimited` wrappers — not as a change to `DefaultFields` or `Format`.

- Adds `field::truncate::Truncated<V>` (and its visitor `VisitTruncated<V>`), following the exact structure of the existing `field::delimited::Delimited<D, V>` wrapper.
- Adds a `MakeExt::truncated(self, max_len: usize)` combinator.
- String and `fmt::Debug` field values whose formatted length exceeds `max_len` characters are truncated at a UTF-8 char boundary and suffixed with `...`. Numeric/bool values are left untouched. `Debug` truncation is allocation-free (writes through a small bounded `fmt::Write` adapter); `str` truncation uses a short-lived `String` only when truncation actually occurs.
- Gated behind the existing `alloc` feature (implied by `std`), matching the crate's no_std/alloc conventions.

Because it composes through the existing `FormatFields` blanket impl, no changes to `Format`, `Layer`, or `SubscriberBuilder` are needed — it's consumed purely via the existing `.fmt_fields()` builder method:

```rust
tracing_subscriber::fmt()
    .fmt_fields(tracing_subscriber::fmt::format::DefaultFields::new().truncated(100))
    .init();
```

This is opt-in only; `DefaultFields` and all existing formatters are unchanged.

## Testing

- `cargo build -p tracing-subscriber --all-features`
- `cargo build -p tracing-subscriber --no-default-features --features alloc`
- `cargo test -p tracing-subscriber --all-features` — all passing except two pre-existing, unrelated `chrono_crate` time-formatting failures that reproduce identically on `master` without this change (local timezone/env-dependent, not touched by this PR).
- `cargo test -p tracing-subscriber --all-features --doc` — doctest for `truncated()` passes.
- `cargo doc -p tracing-subscriber --all-features --no-deps` — builds clean.
- New unit tests cover: long string truncation, values below `max_len` left untouched, long `Debug` value truncation, and UTF-8 char-boundary safety with multi-byte characters.

Also added a CHANGELOG entry.

title: tracing-appender has broken symlinks when a relative path is specified
body:
## Bug Report

### Version

```
│   ├── tracing v0.1.44
│   │   ├── tracing-attributes v0.1.31 (proc-macro)
│   │   └── tracing-core v0.1.36
│   ├── tracing-appender v0.2.5
│   │   └── tracing-subscriber v0.3.23
│   │       ├── tracing-core v0.1.36 (*)
│   │       └── tracing-log v0.2.0
│   │           └── tracing-core v0.1.36 (*)
│   └── tracing-subscriber v0.3.23 (*)
└── tracing v0.1.44 (*)
```

### Platform

Linux 7.1.8-1-cachyos SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Crates

tracing-appender v0.2.5

### Description

When using the `latest_symlink` feature added in #3447, if a *relative* path is specified to [`Builder::build`](https://docs.rs/tracing-appender/0.2.5/tracing_appender/rolling/struct.Builder.html#method.build), the symlink also uses the relative path. This results in broken symlinks when a relative path to a directory is specified.

For example, this code:
```rs
let appender = RollingFileAppender::builder()
    .rotation(Rotation::DAILY)
    .filename_prefix("myapp.log")
    .latest_symlink("latest.log")
    .build("./logs")
    .expect("failed to initialize rolling file appender");
```
Results in the symlink `latest.log` to point to `./logs/myapp.log.2019-01-01` while itself already *inside* of the `logs` directory, so it actually points to `./logs/./logs/myapp.log.2019-01-01`, which is invalid.

The workaround is to always specify an absolute path to `Builder::build`. But this should be fixed by providing the correct `path` to `symlink::symlink_file` (either absolute, or fixing the relative path so it's correct):
https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/d9d4c542de10f5d3a711b7a45ffe450fd0666437/tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs#L802-L808

title: instrument annotation prevents clippy::print_stderr and clippy::print_stdout from working

## Bug Report

When `#[instrument]` is applied to a function, clippy no longer picks up uses of `eprintln!`, `eprint!`, `println!`, `print!` when linting for `clippy::print_stderr` or `clippy::print_stdout`, respectively.

The workaround I am using is to do `#[cfg_attr(not(clippy), instrument)]`, however this is not ideal.

In this [Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=602f6152581b38847847680d83645a62) pick `Tools > Clippy` for an example of the bug, and the workaround.

title: Allow pass non-static level for `event!`
body:
## Feature Request

### Crates

<!--
If known, please specify the tracing crate or crates the new feature should
be added to. Otherwise, delete this section.
-->
* `tracing`

### Motivation

<!--
Please describe the use case(s) or other motivation for the new feature.
-->

Define in runtime, which event level is needed without external match. At the moment in such cases it lead to long and complex `match` or `if` expression, which lead to copy-paste errors.

The only thing which makes it impossible to use  is `static __CALLSITE` creation: `static __CALLSITE: $crate::callsite::DefaultCallsite = $crate::callsite2!` at `tracing-0.1.44/src/macros.rs:885:9`.

Additional motivation: https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/issues/3585

### Proposal

<!--
How should the new feature be implemented, and why? Add any considered
drawbacks.
-->

in outer level: 

```rust
let t_level: tracing::Level = app_level.into();

tracing::event!(t_level, {field = %value}) // see example below for the main reasoning.
```

### Alternatives

<!--
Are there other ways to solve this problem that you've considered? What are
their potential drawbacks? Why was the proposed solution chosen over these
alternatives?
-->

One can use long copy-paste error-prone match case as shown below. there's no possibility to pass other parameters either to reduce maintenance burden, as most of them are part of the same static `__CALLSITE` expression.

```rust
/// Return app level for specific event.
fn obtain_level(/*...*/) -> app::Level { app:Level::Error };

// ...
match obtain_level() {
    Level::Error => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::ERROR, {field = %value}), // could be quite complex expression
    Level::Warn => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::WARN, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
    Level::Info => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::INFO, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
    Level::Debug => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::DEBUG, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
    Level::Trace => tracing::event!(tracing::Level::TRACE, {field = %value}), // copy-paste
}
```

body:
## Bug Report

### Version

At least `0.1.36` and `main`

### Platform

`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, but likely affects all

### Crates

`tracing-core`

### Description

On any of these Rust versions, the test fails the same way:

* `rustc 1.97.0 (2d8144b78 2026-07-07)`
* `rustc 1.98.0-beta.2 (08d5b675a 2026-07-12)`
* `rustc 1.99.0-nightly (77cf889bc 2026-07-12)`

```
---- metadata::tests::level_filter_reprs stdout ----

thread 'metadata::tests::level_filter_reprs' (1481526) panicked at tracing-core/src/metadata.rs:1119:13:
assertion `left == right` failed: repr changed for LevelFilter::OFF
  left: 5
 right: 18446744073709551615
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

Note that `OFF = LevelFilter(None)`. The test has a mapping array that includes `(LevelFilter::OFF, LevelInner::Error as usize + 1)`, which is assuming that `None` fills the niche in the next greater value not used by `Level`. This was never guaranteed, and Rust 1.97 started to prefer wrapping the other way, choosing -1 for `None` in this case.

appender: introduce monthly rotation
body:
## Motivation

While configuring tracing-appender, I wanted to specify a monthly log rotation interval. I was unable to do so, as the largest rotation interval was weekly.

## Solution

Before my introduction of monthly log rotation, the `next_date()` function was straightforward: we could simply add a fixed `Duration` to the current date. However, we cannot do that for months as they do not all have the same `Duration`.

To go to next_month, we edit the current date, setting the month to next month and adding 1 to the year if next month is also crossing a year. We also need to set the day to 1 as the day of current date may not exist next month (eg. when current date is January 31st, next month can't be set to February 31st as this date is invalid). This gives us consistent date-times that is always during next month.

title: RUSTSEC-2026-0195: Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service
body:
> Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service

| Details             |                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Package             | `quick-xml`                      |
| Version             | `0.26.0`                   |
| URL                 | [https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/970](https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/970) |
| Date                | 2026-06-29                         |
| Patched versions    | `>=0.41.0`                  |

`NsReader` resolves namespaces by calling `NamespaceResolver::push` for every
`Start`/`Empty` event *before* the event is returned to the caller. `push`
iterated all `xmlns` / `xmlns:*` attributes on the start tag and, for each one,
appended the prefix bytes to an internal buffer and pushed a `NamespaceBinding`
(32 bytes on 64-bit) to an internal `Vec`, with no upper bound on the number of
declarations.

## Impact

A start tag with `N` namespace declarations drove roughly `3×` the tag's byte
size in `NamespaceResolver` heap, allocated *inside* `quick-xml` before the
`NsReader` consumer ever received the event and could inspect or reject it. A
consumer that bounds its *input* size therefore still cannot bound this
allocation: an `M`-byte start tag yields on the order of `3 × M` bytes of
resolver heap the caller never sees.

On untrusted XML this lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker force large heap
allocations with a single start tag. With several `NsReader`s running
concurrently on independent inputs (a common server pattern), the allocations
stack and can exhaust process memory, causing the operating system to kill the
process (OOM). This was confirmed against a real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet
Labs Routinator), where concurrent RRDP validation workers parsing a crafted
`snapshot.xml` exceeded the memory limit and the process was OOM-killed.

## Affected code paths

Consumers using `NsReader` (which always calls `NamespaceResolver::push` before
yielding `Start`/`Empty`), or calling `NamespaceResolver::push` directly. A plain
`Reader` that does not perform namespace resolution is not affected.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`. `NamespaceResolver::push` now rejects a start
tag that declares more than `DEFAULT_MAX_DECLARATIONS_PER_ELEMENT` (256)
namespace bindings, returning the new `NamespaceError::TooManyDeclarations`
instead of allocating without limit. The limit is configurable via
`NamespaceResolver::set_max_declarations_per_element` (use `usize::MAX` to
restore the previous unbounded behavior), and `NsReader::resolver_mut()` is
provided to reach it.

There is no clean workaround for `NsReader` consumers before 0.41.0, as the
allocation happens inside the reader with no configuration knob to cap it.

See [advisory page](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0195.html) for additional details.

title: RUSTSEC-2026-0194: Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names
body:
> Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names

| Details             |                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Package             | `quick-xml`                      |
| Version             | `0.26.0`                   |
| URL                 | [https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/969](https://github.com/tafia/quick-xml/issues/969) |
| Date                | 2026-06-29                         |
| Patched versions    | `>=0.41.0`                  |

`BytesStart::attributes()` returns an `Attributes` iterator which, by default
(`with_checks(true)`), rejects a start tag that repeats an attribute name. For
each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

See [advisory page](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0194.html) for additional details.

title: fix: point appender symlink to correct target
body:
The latest_symlink feature added to tracing-appender is creating a symlink pointing to an invalid target.

Here is a simple example that shows the issue:

```rust
use tracing_appender::rolling::{RollingFileAppender, Rotation};

fn main() {
    let file_appender = RollingFileAppender::builder()
        .rotation(Rotation::DAILY)
        .filename_prefix("myapp.log")
        .latest_symlink("myapp.log")
        .build("logs")
        .expect("initializing rolling file appender failed");

    tracing_subscriber::fmt().with_writer(file_appender).init();
}
```

and here is the resulting symlink:

```sh
$ cargo run
$ ls -l logs
lrwxrwxrwx 1 aurel aurel 25 30 juin  18:22 myapp.log -> logs/myapp.log.2026-06-30
-rw-rw-r-- 1 aurel aurel  0 30 juin  18:22 myapp.log.2026-06-30
```

Note that both the log file and the symlink are inside the `logs` directory but the symlink is pointing to `logs/myapp.log.2026-06-30` instead of `myapp.log.2026-06-30`.

This patch fixes the issue and generate the proper symlink as shown here:

```sh
$ cargo run
$ ls -l logs
lrwxrwxrwx 1 aurel aurel 20 30 juin  18:24 myapp.log -> myapp.log.2026-06-30
-rw-rw-r-- 1 aurel aurel  0 30 juin  18:24 myapp.log.2026-06-30
```

title: subscriber: cap per-layer-filter callsite interest at `sometimes`
body:
## Motivation

`Filtered<L, F>` carries each filter's per-call decision from `Layer::enabled` to `Layer::on_new_span`/`on_event` via the thread-local `FilterState` bitmap. That side-channel assumes `enabled()` runs immediately before `on_new_span`/`on_event` for the same metadata. When a callsite caches `Interest::always`, the `tracing` macros skip `enabled()` entirely — so `on_new_span` reads whatever the *previous* `enabled()` call (for unrelated metadata) wrote, and the span is silently dropped from every per-layer-filtered layer.

The common production trigger is `log::log_enabled!` via `tracing-log`'s `LogTracer`, which calls `dispatch.enabled()` with per-call dynamic metadata that bypasses callsite caching. Any crate that does this between two `#[instrument]`ed calls — sqlx's `QueryLogger` does after every query — leaves stale disabled bits in `FilterState`, and the next `Interest::always` span never reaches the OTel/fmt/etc. layer it was meant for.

Fixes: #2519
Refs: #3516, #2448, #2704

## Solution

`Registry::register_callsite` now caps the per-layer-filter interest sum at `Interest::sometimes`. Callsites that every per-layer filter accepts get `sometimes` instead of `always`, so `enabled()` runs on every dispatch and `FilterState` is always fresh when `did_enable` reads it. Callsites any filter rejects are unaffected (`never` if all reject, `sometimes` if mixed — same as before).

**Trade-off.** This removes the `Interest::always` fast-path for callsites every per-layer filter accepts. Those callsites now pay one `Filter::enabled()` call per dispatch instead of zero — for the common filters (`LevelFilter`, `Targets`, `EnvFilter` with static directives) that's a level compare plus a target prefix match, plus one thread-local write in `Filtered::enabled`. Stacks without per-layer filters are entirely unaffected. The four `*_interests_are_cached` tests are updated to reflect the new invariant: rejected callsites still cache as `never`; accepted callsites are re-evaluated per dispatch.

Users are already paying a comparable cost via the "add a no-op layer" workaround ([transact-rs/sqlx#3751](https://github.com/transact-rs/sqlx/issues/3751#issuecomment-4131222109)), which makes *rejected* callsites `sometimes` instead. This PR is cheaper for the typical case where rejected callsites outnumber accepted ones, and it doesn't depend on a follow-up event being dispatched to reset the bits.

**Scope.** This fixes the bare-`enabled()` trigger of #3516 — `LogTracer`, the `enabled!`/`event_enabled!` macros, or any direct `dispatch.enabled()` that isn't followed by a dispatch. It does **not** fix the re-entrancy triggers (#2448, #2704), where a layer's `on_event` emits its own event and the inner pass's `enabled()` clobbers `FilterState` bits the outer pass hasn't consumed yet. That case has `enabled()` called fresh; the staleness is from nesting, not skipping, and fixing it needs `FilterState` to be a stack (or the API rework #3516 discusses). This PR doesn't attempt that — it makes the existing mechanism sound for the non-re-entrant case at the cost of the fast-path, and leaves the deeper fix for #3516.

**Testing.** New `tests/layer_filters/stale_filter_state.rs` reproduces #2519: two per-layer-filtered layers, a span both accept (cached `always` before this PR), then a bare `dispatch.enabled()` both reject, then a second span both accept. Before this PR the second span never reached either layer's `on_new_span`; with it, both spans do.

tracing: accept dotted field names as the first field with name:
body:
## Motivation

The level macros (`trace!`, `debug!`, `info!`, `warn!`, `error!`) fail to
compile when a dotted field name (e.g. `order.id`) is the **first** field and
the `name:` specifier is used:

```rust
info!(name: "order.received.ok", order.id = 123, "order received");
// error: local ambiguity when calling macro `info`:
//        multiple parsing options: built-in NTs tt ('field') or 1 other option.
```

`event!` accepts this form, and the level macros accept it when a non-dotted
field comes first or when `name:` is omitted — it is only the `name:` arms that
reject a dotted first field.

The `name:` arms matched fields with a single coarse pattern,
`$($k:ident).+ $($field:tt)*`, with no separator between the field path and the
rest. When the first field is dotted, the `.` is ambiguous: the macro cannot
tell whether it continues the field path (`$($k).+`) or begins `$($field)*`.
The `parent:` and no-specifier arms avoid this by matching `=`/`,`-separated
fields with separate arms (as @hds noted in the issue).

Fixes: #3407

## Solution

Make the `name:` arms granular in the same way as the `parent:`/no-specifier
arms — across all five level macros and all four `name:` combinations (`name`;
`name` + `target`; `name` + `parent`; `name` + `target` + `parent`). For plain,
`?`, and `%` fields, each coarse arm becomes three:

* `$($k:ident).+ = $($field:tt)*` — `field = value`
* `$($k:ident).+, $($field:tt)*` — a shorthand field followed by more
* `$($k:ident).+` — a trailing shorthand field with no value

This resolves the ambiguity while preserving every previously-accepted form.

Adds regression tests covering a dotted first field after `name:` for each
level macro and each `name:` combination (compile-only, matching the existing
`tests/macros.rs` convention).

title: appender: gate symlink support to platforms that support it
body:
## Motivation

`tracing-appender` 0.2.5 added the `latest_symlink` builder option (#3447), which
depends on the [`symlink`](https://crates.io/crates/symlink) crate. That crate
only defines `symlink_file` and `remove_symlink_file` on `unix`, `windows`, and
`redox`, so on other targets — notably `wasm32-unknown-unknown` — the appender no
longer compiles:

```
error[E0425]: cannot find function `remove_symlink_file` in crate `symlink`
   --> tracing-appender/src/rolling.rs:804:26
    |
804 |         let _ = symlink::remove_symlink_file(&symlink_path);
    |                          ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ not found in `symlink`
note: found an item that was configured out
    |
133 | #[cfg(any(target_os = "redox", unix, windows))]
```

tracing-appender 0.2.4 built fine on `wasm32`; 0.2.5 regressed.

Fixes: #3536

## Solution

Gate the `symlink` dependency to the platforms that support symbolic links, and
gate the code that uses it the same way:

- In `Cargo.toml`, move `symlink` into
  `[target.'cfg(any(unix, windows, target_os = "redox"))'.dependencies]`.
- In `rolling.rs`, extract the symlink logic from `create_writer` into an
  `update_latest_symlink` helper with two `cfg`-gated definitions: the real one
  for symlink-capable targets, and a no-op for the rest. `test_latest_symlink`
  is gated the same way.

On platforms without symbolic-link support, `latest_symlink` is now a no-op (the
log file is still written; no symlink is created), and the crate compiles again.
The existing `test-build-wasm` CI job builds `tracing-appender` for `wasm32`.

title: subscriber: don't abort in release when cloning a closed span
body:
## Motivation

`Registry::clone_span` asserts via `assert_ne!` that a span's reference count is
non-zero before incrementing it. Holding a span open across an `.await` point —
incorrect, but easy to do by accident — can leave a stale entry on the span
stack after the span's reference count has reached zero. A later `Span::current()`
then calls `clone_span` on the now-closed span, and the `assert_ne!` aborts the
worker thread, **even in release builds**:

```
thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked at .../registry/sharded.rs:
assertion `left != right` failed: tried to clone a span (Id(...)) that already closed
```

This started when #3289 removed the `clone_span`/`try_close` balancing from the
`Registry`'s `enter`/`exit` — that change didn't account for spans entered
across `.await` points. Entering a span across an await point is incorrect usage,
but it should not crash the program.

Fixes: #3514

## Solution

Downgrade the assertion to `debug_assert_ne!`, as suggested in the issue: debug
builds still surface the misuse during development, while release builds keep
running instead of aborting. Keeping the `fetch_add` leaves the reference count
balanced, so a later `try_close` still removes the span normally.

A regression test reproduces the zero-reference-count clone against a bare
`Registry` and checks the debug-vs-release behavior. Note that only the release
branch distinguishes this fix from the previous `assert_ne!` (both panic under
debug), so it must be run with `cargo test --release` to exercise the
non-aborting path.

title: appender: don't over-prune log files on restart
body:
## Motivation

A `RollingFileAppender` configured with `max_log_files(n)` can delete one more
log file than configured. When the appender is constructed and the current
rotation period's log file already exists — e.g. the application restarted
within the same period, after an upgrade or a crash — startup pruning reduces
the directory to `n - 1` files instead of `n`, silently dropping a log the
user expected to keep.

`Inner::prune_old_logs` always deleted down to `n - 1`, on the assumption that
a new log file was about to be created. That holds when rotating to a new
period, but on restart the writer *appends* to the already-existing
current-period file rather than creating a new one, so the reserved slot is
never filled.

Fixes: #3496

## Solution

Pass the name of the file that is about to be written into `prune_old_logs`,
remove it from the deletion candidates, and reserve exactly one slot for it.
Retention is then reliably `max_files` across both startup and rotation, and
the rotation path is unchanged.

As a side benefit, the file currently being written can no longer be deleted
even if the filesystem's creation timestamps are unreliable, since it is no
longer a deletion candidate.

A regression test (`test_max_log_files_keeps_files_on_restart`) is added, and
the now-stale note in the `max_log_files` docs recommending `m + 1` to work
around the dip below the maximum is removed.

title: subscriber: Replace OFF with None in empty Vec max_level_hint
body:
The expected behavior of adding an empty Vec as Layer is that it does nothing. Right now, it adds a LevelFilter::OFF rule, thus supressing other layers.

This change makes max_level_hint return None, which doesn't supress other layers, following expected behavior.

* Fixes #3563
* This is a breaking change (no API change, but observable behavior)

## Motivation

* Fixes #3563

## Solution

We return `None` when the vec is empty.

### Details

The one-liner: cute solution, but might not be obvious how it works at first glance:

* We want the highest level filter for `LevelFilter`, but we want the `None` case to be even higher priority than other.
* **Problem**: the `Ord` impl of `Option` makes `None` the lowest possible value. **Solution**: We use `min` instead of `max`!
* **Problem**: But then our ordering is invalid for `LevelFilter`. **Solution**: We use `.map(Reverse)` so that `min` for `LevelFilter` is equivalent to `max`!
* We just have to unwrap the whole thing at the end with `Some(x??.0)`

title: Should `<Vec as Layer>::max_level_hint` be OFF when Vec is empty?
body:
## Bug Report

### Crates

* `tracing_subscriber`

### Version

* tracing-subscriber v0.3.23
* tracing-appender v0.2.5
* tracing v0.1.44
* tracing-core v0.1.36

### Platform

Linux 6.17.0

### The problem

Following (more or less) #2499, I added my own `Vec<Box<dyn Layer<..>>>` as a layer. The end result looks somewhat like that:

```rust
    let dyn_layers: Vec<Box<dyn Layer<...>>> = vec![];
    tracing_subscriber::registry()
        .with(dyn_layers)
        .with(env_filter_layer)
        .with(non_blocking_logger)
        .init();
```

I expected it to be the same as without the `.with(dyn_layers)`, instead, when adding `dyn_layers`, all other layers stopped working.

### The reason

I believe that's because  `<Vec as Layer>::max_level_hint` returns `LevelFilter::OFF` when the `Vec` is empty, which apparently turns of all events for all the other loggers (I'm not quite clear on the semantics of `.with`, I thought it shouldn't, even with `LevelFilter::OFF`)

### My Workaround

I initialize `dyn_layers` with a `Identity`, ensuring that it not toggle off log levels:

```rust
    let dyn_layers: Vec<Box<dyn Layer<...>>> = vec![Box::new(Identity::new()) as _];
    tracing_subscriber::registry()
        .with(dyn_layers)
        .with(env_filter_layer)
        .with(non_blocking_logger)
        .init();
```

### Context

My actual setup is more complex, plus I have a couple layers wrapped in a `reload::Layer`, but I don't think it should influence the result.

title: Opt-in compile-time check for duplicate field names in event!/span! macros?
body:
## Summary

Would the maintainers be open to an opt-in cargo feature (e.g. `strict-field-names`) that makes the `event!`, `span!`, `info!`, etc. macros fail to **compile** when the same field name appears more than once in a single call?

Asking before sending a PR to gauge interest.

## Current behavior

`tracing` today silently accepts duplicate field names in a single macro invocation. Reproducer:

```rust
info!(foo = 1, foo = 2);
info!(http.method = "GET", http.method = "POST");
```

Observed (verified against current `main`):

- `Event::metadata().fields().len() == 2` — both entries present in the `FieldSet`.
- The visitor receives two `record_*` calls, both with `Field::name() == "foo"` (different indices).
- `FieldSet::field("foo")` returns the first occurrence only (`position(|f| f == name)` in `tracing-core/src/field.rs`), so name-based lookup silently ignores the second.
- No warning, no diagnostic.

This is almost always a programmer mistake — the user typed the same key twice — and is currently invisible until it surfaces in a downstream subscriber (or doesn't, depending on the visitor).

## Proposal

A cargo feature on `tracing` (and matching support in `tracing-attributes` for `#[instrument(fields(...))]`) that, when enabled, emits a compile-time assertion alongside the existing callsite metadata, using a `const fn` over the `&'static str` field names already produced by `fieldset!`. MSRV-safe (`const` panic since 1.57). Off by default to preserve compatibility.

## Motivation

This came up while working on `opentelemetry-rust`, where the OpenTelemetry spec requires log/span attributes to be a map of unique keys. The SDK is debating whether to dedupe at runtime on the hot path (perf cost) or push the responsibility to producers. For the within-callsite case, a compile-time check in `tracing` would eliminate one whole class of duplicates at source. References: open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust#3497, open-telemetry/opentelemetry-rust#3498.

## Question

Before writing a PR — is this something the maintainers would consider merging if implemented cleanly and gated behind an off-by-default feature? Or is the preference to keep this kind of check out of `tracing` core (e.g. leave it to a clippy lint or external proc-macro wrapper)?

Happy to send a draft PR if there's interest.

title: attributes: support value transformations `#[instrument(err)]` and `ret`
body:
This lets users transform the logged value by supplying a closure to `#[instrument(err)]` or `#[instrument(ret)]`:

```rust
#[instrument(err(Display, |err| err.as_ref()))]
fn foo() -> Result<(), mylib::Error> { ... }
```

Closes #3560

title: `#[instrument(err)]` can't produce a `&(dyn Error + 'static)` (for `tracing_opentelemetry`)
body:
## Feature Request

### Crates

- `tracing-attributes`

### Motivation

`#[instrument(err)]` logs the `error` field as either `Debug` or `Display`, but in order for [`tracing_opentelemetry::OpenTelemetryLayer::with_error_fields_to_exceptions`](https://docs.rs/tracing-opentelemetry/latest/tracing_opentelemetry/struct.OpenTelemetryLayer.html#method.with_error_fields_to_exceptions) to correctly set the `exception.message` and `exception.stacktrace` fields, the `error` field needs to be a `&(dyn Error + 'static)`.

Error return types are usually not a `&(dyn Error + 'static)`, so we need some way to transform the error type into that value, e.g. ([for `anyhow::Error`](https://docs.rs/anyhow/latest/anyhow/struct.Error.html#impl-AsRef%3Cdyn+Error+%2B+Send+%2B+Sync%3E-for-Error)) `AsRef::as_ref`. But this won't be the same for all types, so we should have some way of transforming the error before it's logged.

### Proposal

IMO this request is straightforward, and I'm interested in implementing it, but the syntax is the tricky part. I don't have strong opinions on the syntax here; see below for some options I've thought about.

### Alternatives

#### Closure

```rust
﻿#[instrument(err(|e| e.as_ref()))]
```

Here we let the user pass a _closure_ for transforming the error before it's logged. This doesn't hardcode any names, it's compatible with existing arguments, and makes the semantics clear.

#### Match-like

```rust
#[instrument(err(error => error.as_ref()))]
```

This says that we transform the `error` by calling `error.as_ref()` before returning it.

This syntax is a special duck; it isn't used anywhere else, and it doesn't match the form of other 'arguments' for this macro using parenthesis.

The `error =>` prefix could be mandatory, or it could be used to specify a name for the `Err` variable in the invocation (i.e. `err => err.as_ref()` could also be allowed).


#### Fields

```rust
#[instrument(err(fields(error = error.as_ref())))]
```

We could reuse the `fields` syntax for this, treating a field named `error` as a special value. This is hardcoded and kind of unintuitive; it doesn't work like plain `#[instrument(fields(...))]` does.

See:
- #3076

#### A new argument

```rust
#[instrument(err(value(err.as_ref())))]
```

Here, we hardcode a name (`err`) and let the user specify the `error` field's value with an expression.

This could be combined with the "match-like" syntax for more flexibility.

This syntax has the advantage of "looking like" the rest of the arguments and not introducing any new syntactic concepts.

title: core: change get_default to accept FnOnce instead of FnMut
body:
Changes `get_default` in both std and no_std variants to accept `FnOnce` instead of `FnMut`.

Since the closure is only ever called once, `FnOnce` is the correct bound here. This is a backwards-compatible change since every `FnMut` is also `FnOnce`.

Closes #1653

title: attributes: Improve spans for body block
body:
<!--
Thank you for your Pull Request. Please provide a description above and review
the requirements below.

Bug fixes and new features should include tests.

Contributors guide: https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md
-->

## Motivation

`tracing::instrument` expands to something approximately like this:

```
fn name() {//^0
  {//^1
    // span
    {//^2
      if false {}
      {//^3
        // actual statements from the body
      }
    }
  }
}
```

When the actual body contains errors, rustc will use all kinds of spans to display those errors.

Currently, tracing will assign call-site spans to `^1`, `^2`, `^3` and the spans from the real `{` to `^0`. This is a problem because rustc will sometimes use the span from `^3` in syntax errors:

```
fn main() {
    let x:
}
```

```
error: expected type, found `}`
 --> src/main.rs:4:1
  |
3 |     let x:
  |          - while parsing the type for `x`
4 | }
  | ^ expected type

error: expected type, found `}`
 --> src/main.rs:1:1
  |
1 | #[tracing_attributes::instrument]
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected type
2 | fn main() {
3 |     let x:
  |          - while parsing the type for `x`
  |
  = note: this error originates in the attribute macro `tracing_attributes::instrument` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)
```

The first error is from pre-expansion parsing, while the second error comes from post-expansion parsing and chas the bad span because rustc tries to point at the `}` character.


## Solution

By making `^3` use the user token span as well, the span of the error will improve significantly.

```
error: expected type, found `}`
 --> src/main.rs:2:11
  |
2 |   fn main() {
  |  ___________^
3 | |     let x:
  | |          - while parsing the type for `x`
4 | | }
  | |_^ expected type
```

It's still not perfect because of limitations in `proc_macro::Group` that do not allow assigning the open and close spans separately. If that ever becomes available, syn should be able to use it automatically and tracing would get the nice errors.

Because it's still not quite perfect after this change, errors will still not be deduplicated and there will be two of them.

An alternative would be to preserve the entire body, including the `{}`, verbatim without any syn-printing, which I think should be able to preserve the spans precisely. I opted against this for now as it would involve slightly more changes.

title: feat: `TracedError` impl Clone, get inner error

## Motivation

`TracedError` currently does not `impl Clone`, even if the inner error implements `Clone`.

Additionally, there is currently no way to access the inner error.

Adds `impl Clone for TracedError` and two new methods, one for accessing the inner error by reference and one for "unwrapping" the `TracedError` entirely.

title: subscriber: Change Writer's `with_ansi*` accessors to pub
body:
This PR changes the scope of the `with_ansi*` accessors in the `Writer` class from `pub(crate)` to `pub`. 

## Motivation

Our software's workflow maps a subscriber's events to a `Writer` class for writing stdout and stderr to an HTML file. While the subscriber layer itself can set `with_ansi_sanitization` to false (thereby giving us "clean" output), the writer instead holds its own state. This caused some confusion when the `Writer` ended up writing codes, when the output to the console did not.

```
let report_layer = tracing_subscriber::fmt::layer()
                .with_target(print_target)
                .with_writer(report_writer)
                .pretty()
                .with_ansi(true)
                .map_event_format(move |e| {
                    let f = e
                        .with_ansi(true)
                        .with_source_location(print_source_location);
                    FormatHtml::new(f, converter) // <-- This holds a Writer
                })
                .with_ansi_sanitization(false);   // <-- which makes this useless in the Writer context
```


## Solution

Make the accessors public so that we can modify the `Writer` behavior to match the layer from which it is mapped. Happy to hear other solutions, but given the discussion in the file, it seems like this may have been on your minds anyway.
